title: Florida Condo Special Assessments: What Buyers Should Check in 2026
dek: December 31 is the last deadline for many older condo buildings to finish their safety inspections and reserve studies. Before you buy, it pays to know what that means for prices, how big assessments get and which documents to read.
body:
Special assessments are common in Florida condos right now, and they can be large. Roughly two in five Florida condo owners have faced one in the past three years, according to property manager TrueNorth. Most run from a few thousand dollars to tens of thousands per unit, and in the worst cases, older South Florida towers have billed owners more than $100,000 each.

You can see most of that risk before you buy. Florida now requires older condo buildings to get a structural inspection and a reserve study, and you are entitled to read both. The trick is reading them before your contract locks you in.

Why December 31, 2026 matters for condo buyers

After the Surfside collapse in 2021, Florida added two requirements for condo buildings three or more habitable stories tall:

  • A milestone inspection. A structural inspection by an engineer or architect, due by December 31 of the year the building turns 30, then every 10 years.
  • A structural integrity reserve study (SIRS). A study of the roof, structure, plumbing, waterproofing and other big items that sets how much the association has to save each year to replace them.

Owners have not been allowed to vote to waive SIRS reserve funding since the end of 2024. Buildings that are due for a milestone inspection could do both at once, with December 31, 2026 as the outside deadline. That is why many boards are finishing their numbers, and their assessments, this fall.

The state's first look at the results came in July 2026. Florida's legislative research office, OPPAGA, counted 8,736 completed phase one milestone inspections in 2024 and 2025, and 1,575 phase two inspections. A phase two means the engineer found signs of real deterioration that need a closer look, which is often where big repair bills start.

How big do Florida condo special assessments get?

It depends almost entirely on the building's age, how close it sits to salt water, and how little it saved in the past. Newer buildings with healthy reserves may see nothing beyond higher monthly dues. Older coastal buildings with years of deferred repairs are where the headline numbers come from. Axios Miami reported a $30 million assessment at the Cricket Club in North Miami, about $134,000 per owner, on a building nearly 50 years old.

It isn't only Miami. A Sarasota agent, Team Renick, reports that several communities on Longboat Key and in downtown Sarasota have levied assessments of $20,000 to $80,000 per owner, and that Siesta Key buildings with thin reserves have faced $25,000 to $60,000 or more. On Sand Key in Clearwater Beach, the 12 story South Beach III building was evacuated in May 2025 when workers repairing the garage found cracks in a support column, even though an engineering evaluation the previous fall had found the building safe. A clean inspection tells you where a building stands today, not what the next repair will cost.

The 2025 condo law gave associations some breathing room. After a milestone inspection, a board can pause SIRS reserve contributions for two budget years to pay for the repairs the inspection found. That can soften the hit, but the repair bill still has to be paid.

Are Florida condo prices dropping?

Slowly. The statewide median condo and townhome price was $290,000 in October 2026, down 3.3% from a year earlier, with about 8 months of supply on the market, according to Florida Realtors. More choice and softer prices are good for you, as long as you know why a particular unit is cheap.

In some beach towns a condo costs a fraction of a house, which is good news if you're buying on a budget. It also means more homework: the cheapest units are often in older buildings, and those are the ones these rules hit hardest. What to ask for before you buy a Florida condo

When you buy a resale condo in Florida, the law entitles you to a set of association records at the seller's expense, including the annual financial statement and budget, the latest SIRS and the milestone inspection summary. Ask for them on day one and read them before your review period ends.

  • The milestone inspection summary. Look for whether a phase two inspection was required, what repairs were listed, and whether they have started. Florida now requires repairs to begin within 365 days of a phase two report.
  • The SIRS and its funding schedule. Compare what the study says the association should save each year with what the budget actually collects. A big gap is a future assessment. You can also look the building up yourself: on myfloridalicense.com, open the Division of Condominiums' SIRS Reporting page and search the association's name. Only complete SIRS submissions show up there, so a building that isn't listed is a question to ask, not proof it skipped the study.
  • The estoppel certificate. It itemizes every regular and special assessment owed and scheduled on the unit. Unpaid assessments follow the unit to the new owner.
  • The last 12 months of board minutes. Talk of loans, engineers, concrete or roof bids usually shows up here before it shows up as a bill.
  • The association website. Since January 1, 2026, associations with 25 or more units must post their financial records, SIRS and other key documents online for owners.
  • Your lender's answer on the building. Some buildings with deferred repairs or low reserves no longer qualify for conventional loans. Ask your lender to check the building early, before you pay for an inspection.
  • An insurance quote for the unit. The master policy covers the building, but you still need your own condo policy, and in many towns your own flood coverage. See what insurance costs by county and our flood rankings.

You also get time to back out. Since July 2025, a Florida resale condo contract gives the buyer 7 days, not counting weekends and legal holidays, to cancel after receiving the association documents, up from 3 days before. If the seller never delivers the required inspection and SIRS paperwork, the contract is voidable at your option before closing. Ask your agent to put the document delivery date in writing so you know exactly when the clock starts.

Which Florida condos avoid the new rules?

The milestone inspection and SIRS rules apply to buildings three or more habitable stories tall. Low rise condos, villas and townhomes under that height are outside them, and buildings under 30 years old won't need a milestone inspection yet. That doesn't make them risk free, since every association still has to maintain its property, but it removes the biggest source of surprise bills this year.

If you love a particular high rise, the good news is that the buildings that already did their homework are easy to spot: a recent milestone inspection with no phase two, a SIRS with reserves funded to plan, and minutes that are boring. Those are the buildings worth paying a little more for. For other costs that never show up on a listing, see the bills not on the listing.
faq: What is a special assessment on a Florida condo?

A one time charge to every owner on top of regular dues, usually to pay for a major repair the reserves can't cover. Your share is normally set by your unit's ownership percentage in the condo declaration.
How long do I have to cancel a Florida condo purchase after getting the documents?
On a resale, 7 days after you receive the association documents, not counting weekends and legal holidays. The window was 3 days before July 2025.
What is the Florida condo deadline on December 31, 2026?
It is the outside deadline for buildings due for a milestone inspection to finish it together with their structural integrity reserve study (SIRS).
Which Florida condos need a milestone inspection?
Buildings three or more habitable stories tall, by December 31 of the year the building turns 30 and every 10 years after that.
Are Florida condo prices going down?
Slightly. The statewide median condo and townhome price was $290,000 in October 2026, down 3.3% from a year earlier, with about 8 months of supply, per Florida Realtors.
Can a buyer see the SIRS before buying a Florida condo?
Yes. On a resale, Florida law entitles the buyer to the latest SIRS and the milestone inspection summary, along with the budget and financial statement, at the seller's expense.
